items.stem: What is meant by dissolving?
items.answer: The mixing of a solid into a liquid so that its particles spread between the particles of the liquid
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Dissolving – the mixing of a solid into a liquid so that its particles spread between the particles of the liquid.

items.stem: The smell of incense sticks reaches us across a room because of:
items.answer: diffusion of the scent particles in air
items.markingKey: (a) diffusion of the scent particles in air.
options: diffusion of the scent particles in air

items.stem: Why does the smell of hot food reach us faster than that of cold food?
items.answer: At higher temperature particles move faster, so the smell particles diffuse faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster particles. 1 mark: faster diffusion.

items.stem: Saanvi dissolved 2–3 crystals of potassium permanganate in 100 mL of water and then diluted it 6 times, each time taking 10 mL and adding 90 mL of water. The last solution is still faintly coloured. What does this tell us about the particles in one crystal?
items.answer: One crystal contains millions of tiny particles that keep dividing into still smaller ones.
items.markingKey: Even after 6 dilutions (by 10 each time, i.e. 10^6), colour remains: the crystal must contain an enormous number of very small particles (2 marks).

items.stem: Ishaan dissolved 2–3 crystals of potassium permanganate in 100 mL of water and then diluted it 3 times, each time taking 10 mL and adding 90 mL of water. The last solution is still faintly coloured. What does this tell us about the particles in one crystal?
items.answer: One crystal contains millions of tiny particles that keep dividing into still smaller ones.
items.markingKey: Even after 3 dilutions (by 10 each time, i.e. 10^3), colour remains: the crystal must contain an enormous number of very small particles (2 marks).

items.stem: Harpreet dissolved 2–3 crystals of potassium permanganate in 100 mL of water and then diluted it 5 times, each time taking 10 mL and adding 90 mL of water. The last solution is still faintly coloured. What does this tell us about the particles in one crystal?
items.answer: One crystal contains millions of tiny particles that keep dividing into still smaller ones.
items.markingKey: Even after 5 dilutions (by 10 each time, i.e. 10^5), colour remains: the crystal must contain an enormous number of very small particles (2 marks).

items.stem:
Read: Two students placed a drop of blue ink in a beaker of hot water and in a beaker of cold water. In the hot water, the colour spread through the beaker in 2 minutes; in the cold water it took 10 minutes.
(i) Name the process. (ii) Why was it faster in hot water? (iii) Why does it not need stirring? (iv) What would happen in a beaker of honey? Why?
items.answer: (i) Diffusion. (ii) Particles move faster at higher temperature. (iii) Particles of liquids keep moving on their own. (iv) Much slower, because honey is thick and its particles move with difficulty.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Design an activity to show that diffusion is faster at higher temperature. What will you keep the same?
items.answer: Add a drop of ink (or a crystal of potassium permanganate) gently to two beakers, one of hot and one of cold water; observe the spread over time. Keep the same: volume of water, size of drop/crystal, beakers, no stirring.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: set-up. 1 mark: observation. 1 mark: controlled variables.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The spreading and mixing of particles of one substance among those of another on their own."
items.answer: diffusion
items.markingKey: (b) Diffusion is the spreading and mixing of particles of one substance among those of another on their own.

items.stem: When a crystal of potassium permanganate is put in water, the colour spreads. This shows that:
items.answer: matter is made of tiny particles that move
items.markingKey: (a) matter is made of tiny particles that move.
options: matter is made of tiny particles that move

items.stem: A teacher sprays room freshener at one corner. Students near the corner smell it in 5 seconds, those at the far end in 25 seconds. In winter it takes even longer. Explain both observations.
items.answer: Particles diffuse through air and take more time to travel farther; in winter the air is colder and the particles move more slowly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: distance. 1 mark: temperature.

items.stem: When 50 mL of water and 50 mL of alcohol are mixed, the total volume is slightly less than 100 mL. This shows that:
items.answer: there are spaces between particles
items.markingKey: (d) there are spaces between particles.

items.stem: What is meant by a liquid?
items.answer: A state of matter with a fixed volume but no fixed shape, which takes the shape of its container
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A liquid – a state of matter with a fixed volume but no fixed shape, which takes the shape of its container.

items.stem: In which state do particles only vibrate about fixed positions?
items.answer: Solid
items.markingKey: (c) Solid.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Gases have a fixed volume.
Reason (R): Gas particles move freely in all directions.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A false; R true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.answer: A gas: carbon dioxide, oxygen. A liquid: honey, mercury, water.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a liquid at room temperature?
items.answer: steam
items.markingKey: (a) Steam is a gas, not a liquid. Each of the others (water, milk, honey) is a liquid.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a solid at room temperature?
items.answer: water
items.markingKey: (b) Water is a liquid, not a solid. Each of the others (ice cube, wooden block, iron rod) is a solid.

items.stem: With the help of the particle model, describe what happens when ice is heated from −10 °C until it becomes steam. Explain why temperature stays constant at two stages.
items.answer: Ice particles vibrate faster as temperature rises to 0 °C; at 0 °C heat breaks attraction and ice melts, temperature constant; water heats to 100 °C, particles move faster; at 100 °C heat is used to separate particles completely into steam, temperature constant; steam particles move freely.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage (max 4) + 1 mark for explaining constant temperature.

items.stem: Using the particle model, explain why we can smell perfume but not a piece of iron.
items.answer: Perfume is a liquid that evaporates easily, and its particles move into the air and reach our nose; iron particles are tightly held in the solid and do not escape.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: perfume particles escape. 1 mark: iron particles held.

items.stem: Which state has the largest spaces between particles?

items.markingKey: (d) A false; R true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

items.stem: Why is it possible to fill a lot of air into a football with a pump, but impossible to fill much water into a full bottle?
items.answer: Air particles have large spaces and can be pushed closer (compressed); water particles are already close and cannot be compressed much.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: air compressible. 1 mark: water not.

items.stem: Explain why a wooden block keeps its shape but water poured from a jug takes the shape of a glass.
items.answer: Particles in wood are held by strong attraction in fixed positions; in water the attraction is weaker and particles can slide over one another, so it flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strong attraction in solid. 1 mark: liquid flows.

items.stem: Arrange iron, water and air in increasing order of (i) interparticle space and (ii) interparticle attraction. Explain how the order matches their compressibility.
items.answer: (i) Iron < water < air. (ii) Air < water < iron. Larger spaces and weaker attraction make air the most compressible; iron, with the smallest spaces, is hardly compressible.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each order. 1 mark explanation.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The ability of a substance to flow."
items.answer: fluidity
items.markingKey: (b) Fluidity is the ability of a substance to flow.

items.stem: Which is the most compressible?
items.answer: Air
items.markingKey: (c) Air.

items.stem: A balloon is pressed from all sides and becomes smaller, but returns to its size when released. Explain using particles.
items.answer: The air particles are pushed closer into the spaces between them; when released, the fast-moving particles push the walls back out.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: compressed spaces. 1 mark: particles push back.

items.stem: Define boiling.
items.answer: The rapid change of a liquid into a gas throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Boiling – the rapid change of a liquid into a gas throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.

items.stem: On heating, the particles of a solid:
items.answer: vibrate faster and move apart
items.markingKey: (d) vibrate faster and move apart.

items.stem: Why do clothes dry faster on a sunny, windy day?
items.answer: Heat increases evaporation and wind carries away the water vapour, so more water can evaporate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: temperature. 1 mark: wind.

water drops outside a glass of cold water
